newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers locked in stand-off with police.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers locked in stand-off with police.

text.p: Protesting Greek farmers were locked in a tense stand-off with the socialist government on Friday after police deflated the tyres of thousands of tractors lining roads to prevent a fresh road blockade.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis, determined to push through his tough economic policies, refused to bow to a farmers' ultimatum on Thursday to meet them to discuss their demands and vowed to keep the roads open at all costs.
"The government has taken all measures to keep highways free," Simitis told parliament on Friday. "The government will never succumb to blackmail."

Farmers responded to his snub by lining the sides of Greece's main north-south road with 2,000 tractors late on Thursday. Television showed an endless line of headlights moving down the highway, blocking traffic for hours.

But after farmers left a line of tractors about five km (three miles) long by the road near Almyros in central Greece, police cordoned off the area and methodically deflated their tyres to paralyse them.

"Deflating the tyres was an ingenious measure," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told a news briefing. "It was done in the presence of a public prosecutor and those who suffered damages can resort to the courts."
One Greek television reporter was slightly injured when he tried to force his way through riot police to film the operation, eyewitnesses said.
"What the government did is despicable," farmers' representative Vangelis Boutas told reporters. "They want to block our tractors and then force us to talk."
Farmers' representatives were holding meetings on Friday to decide their course of action and have called on farmers to attend a mass rally on Friday evening in Almyros.
They have been inventive in eluding police for the last four days, driving their tractors through vast cotton fields and across rivers to reach key points of the national highway.

Facing critisism for taking no action when the farmers occupied highways for 25 days in December, the government has sent 5,000 police, many in riot gear, into the central Thessaly region with strict orders to keep roads open.
But farmers have been playing cat-and-mouse games, managing to block smaller roads in a bid to show that police could not stop them from repeating their December action.
Simitis had waited out that blockade, saying the country could not afford to satisfy the farmers' demands, which include cheaper fuel, lower taxes and more subsidies.
The farmers gave up the December protest because of the Christmas holidays but vowed to bring their tractors back to highways if their demands were not met.
They are among a long list of groups protesting or striking against a 1997 budget described as the toughest in 15 years, and strict incomes and tax policies.
Teachers are on strike for a third week while labour confederations have staged repeated walkouts against the government. Protest rallies almost daily congest traffic in the Greek capital.
Simitis has turned down all labour demands, saying giving in would risk Greece's efforts to catch up with its European Union partners.
